title: BCD (Binary-Coded Decimal)
summary: BCD (Binary-Coded Decimal) encodes each decimal digit (0-9) as a 4-bit nibble. Packed BCD: two digits per byte (high nibble = tens, low nibble = ones). Unpacked BCD: one digit per byte (low nibble = digit, high nibble = 0 or zone). Used in financial calculations, real-time clocks, and legacy systems.

ext.summary: BCD (Binary-Coded Decimal) encodes each decimal digit (0-9) as a 4-bit nibble. Packed BCD: two digits per byte (high nibble = tens, low nibble = ones). Unpacked BCD: one digit per byte (low nibble = digit, high nibble = 0 or zone). Used in financial calculations, real-time clocks, and legacy systems.

structure.meaning: High nibble = tens digit, low nibble = ones digit. E.g., 0x42 = decimal 42.
Low nibble = digit, high nibble = 0 (or zone nibble 0x3 for ASCII). E.g., 0x04 = digit 4.
For signed BCD: the last nibble can be 0xC (+), 0xD (-), or 0xF (unsigned).

notes: BCD is used in financial calculations (exact decimal arithmetic), RTCs (real-time clocks), and legacy mainframes.
BCD wastes space (4 bits per digit vs 3.32 bits for binary) but avoids binary-decimal conversion errors.
x86 has BCD instructions: DAA (decimal adjust after addition), DAS (after subtraction), AAA, AAS, AAM, AAD.
Packed BCD is used in the RTC (CMOS) for storing time/date.
